- --b is completely ignored: __setattr__('str', b) sets a dead instance attribute, no effect, returns None.
- LINE1 prints str(fragment) as parsed from A.
- LINE2 = fragment.path.add(C) then print str(fragment).
- LINE3 = fragment.path.load(D); fragment.query.load('value'); print str(fragment)  -> query is always literally 'value'.
- LINE4 prints the whole URL with the mutated fragment.
- Fragment str = path + '?' + query when both non-empty, else path+query. When query non-empty, literal '?' chars inside the fragment PATH are escaped to %3F; when query is empty they stay raw.
- furl DECODES percent-escapes on parse and RE-ENCODES on output: '%41%42' -> 'AB'; '%2F' inside a path segment -> stays '%2F'; lone '%' -> '%25'; 'a%zz' -> 'a%25zz'.
- Scheme and host are lowercased. Default ports dropped (http:80, https:443) but non-default kept (http:443 kept).
- URL query: '+' decodes to space, space encodes to '+'. 'a=b&c&d=' round-trips exactly (key-only 'c' vs empty-value 'd=' are distinct).

input.area: Fragment composition: how str(fragment) is built from (path, query, separator), and how f.url decides to emit '#'
rules:
PARSE (Fragment.load). The fragment source text is everything after the FIRST '#' in A (a later '#' belongs to the fragment text itself and is later encoded as %23). If A has no '#', the fragment source is ''. Splitting the fragment source into (path, query) uses this exact algorithm, operating on the RAW, still-percent-encoded text:
  toks = frag.split('?', maxsplit=1)   # at most 2 pieces
  if len(toks) == 1:                    # no '?' anywhere
      if '=' in frag: query.load(frag); path.load('')      # whole thing is the QUERY
      else:           path.load(frag);  query.load('')     # whole thing is the PATH
  else:                                 # there is at least one '?'
      if '=' in toks[1]: path.load(toks[0]); query.load(toks[1])   # split at the first '?'
      else:              path.load(frag); query.load('')           # NO split; the '?' stays inside the PATH

The '=' test is performed on the RAW text before any percent-decoding. '%3D' is NOT an '='. Evidence: '#a%3Db' -> path='a=b' (decoded only afterwards; L2 appends '/c' to it), whereas '#a=b' -> query='a=b' (L2 gives 'c?a=b'). Likewise '#a?b%3Dc' has no '=' in toks[1]='b%3Dc', so the whole 'a?b%3Dc' becomes the path.

maxsplit is exactly 1, verified by '#a?b?c=d': toks[1]='b?c=d' contains '=' so path='a', query='b?c=d' (rendered 'a?b%3Fc=d'). A plain split('?') would have given toks[1]='b' (no '='), i.e. path='a?b?c=d' — not what happens.

Consequences worth memorizing: a fragment that is only '?' -> path='?', query='' (NOT an empty split). '#??' -> path='??'. '#?&' -> path='?&'. '#a?' -> path='a?'. '#a?b' -> path='a?b'. '#?q=1' -> path='', query='q=1'. '#?=' -> path='', query='='. '#=' -> path='', query='='. '#a=b?c' -> path='a=b?c' (toks[1]='c' has no '='). '#a=b?c=d' -> path='a=b', query='c=d'.

COMPOSE (str(fragment)). Let p = str(fragment.path) rendered with the fragment-path encoder (so a literal '?' in the path has already been encoded to '%3F', '#'->'%23', ' '->'%20', '%'->'%25'), and q = str(fragment.query) rendered with the query encoder (' '->'+', '?'->'%3F'). Then:
  if q == '':  return p.replace('%3F', '?')      # un-escape '?' – unambiguous with no query
  if p == '':  return q                          # NO leading '?' separator
  return p + '?' + q

Equivalently as a 2x2 table: (path='', query='') -> ''; (path=P, query='') -> P with every '%3F' turned back into a literal '?'; (path='', query=Q) -> Q verbatim, with no '?' prefix; (path=P, query=Q) -> P + '?' + Q with '?' inside P kept as '%3F'.

The '%3F' -> '?' un-escaping in the query-empty case is applied to the FINAL ENCODED path string, not to the decoded segments. Proof: C='a?b%3Dc' appended to path 'z' gives 'z/a%3Fb%253Dc' when the fragment query is non-empty, but 'z/a?b%253Dc' when it is empty — the '%3F' produced by the path encoder is rewritten while the neighbouring '%25' is untouched. Implement it literally as encoded_path.replace('%3F','?') (the encoder always emits uppercase hex, so a case-insensitive replace is unnecessary).

Only '?' gets this special treatment. '#' stays '%23' in both cases, '%' stays '%25', ' ' stays '%20'. Verified by an exhaustive ASCII 33..126 sweep: the query-empty and query-non-empty renderings of the fragment path are byte-identical for all 94 printable characters EXCEPT '?' ('x?y' vs 'x%3Fy').

'?' characters that live in the fragment QUERY are always percent-encoded to %3F, regardless of whether the path is empty. '#??=' -> path='', query has key '?' -> output '%3F='. '#a?b?c=d' -> 'a?b%3Fc=d'. There is never a case where a '?' inside the query is emitted raw.

SEPARATOR FLAG. furl's Fragment has a `separator` attribute, but it is NOT observable through this program. Every LINE3 output in ~40 different A values (including path-only fragments such as '#a', '#/', '#?', '#a?', and no-fragment URLs) is 'd?value' — i.e. the '?' separator is emitted whenever both path and query are non-empty. Implement str(fragment) as if separator is permanently True; do not model it.

LINE1 = str(fragment) as parsed from A (composition rule above). LINE2 = fragment.path.add(C) then str(fragment); the query parsed from A is preserved, so LINE2 exercises the (non-empty path, non-empty query) branch when A's fragment had a query. LINE3 = fragment.path.load(D); fragment.query.load('value'); then str(fragment) — the query is ALWAYS the literal 'value', so LINE3 is 'value' when D produces an empty path and '<encoded D>?value' otherwise.

URL COMPOSITION / '#' EMISSION. f.url is assembled as: scheme-and-authority + path + ('?' + querystr if querystr != '' else '') + ('#' + fragmentstr if fragmentstr != '' else ''). The '?' half of this rule is directly observable: A='http://h/p?#f' -> LINE4 'http://h/p#d?value' (the empty URL query is dropped, no '?'), while A='?q#f' -> '?q#d?value'.

In THIS program LINE4 always contains a '#'. Because LINE3 forces fragment.query = 'value', str(fragment) is never empty, so the '#' is unconditionally emitted. Verified over 126 (A, D) combinations: zero outputs lacked '#'. With D='' the output is exactly '<url>#value' (no path, no '?'), e.g. A='http://h/p' D='' -> 'http://h/p#value'; A='' D='' -> '#value'.

There is NO observable difference between A having a trailing '#' with nothing after it and A having no '#' at all. `--a 'http://h/p'` and `--a 'http://h/p#'` produce byte-identical 4-line output ('', 'c', 'd?value', 'http://h/p#d?value'). Do not track a 'had a fragment delimiter' flag for output purposes.

Empty / degenerate URLs: A='' , A='#', A='?', A='#?', A='?#' all yield LINE4 = '#d?value' (D='d') or '#value' (D=''). A bare '?' with an empty query is dropped from the output; the '#' is still emitted because the fragment is non-empty. Note A='#?' differs from the others in LINE1/LINE2 only ('?' and '?/c'), because its fragment path is the literal '?'.

Adding to the fragment path (LINE2) never affects '#' emission in LINE4, because LINE3 subsequently replaces the whole fragment path with D. Ordering within one run is strictly: parse A -> print (LINE1) -> path.add(C) -> print (LINE2) -> path.load(D) + query.load('value') -> print (LINE3) -> print f.url (LINE4). LINE4 therefore always reflects the LINE3 state of the fragment.

Fragment path join semantics used by add(C) (needed to reproduce LINE2): the result is the existing path segments with C's segments appended, joined by '/'. '' + 'c' -> 'c'; 'a' + 'c' -> 'a/c'; 'a/' + 'c' -> 'a/c' (a trailing empty segment is absorbed); 'a' + 'c/' -> 'a/c/'; '/' + 'c' -> '/c'; 'a' + '' -> 'a'; '' + '' -> ''; '' + '/' -> '/'.

Round-tripping: the output of str(fragment) re-parses to the same (path, query) under the load algorithm. path-only 'a?' re-parses to path 'a?'; query-only 'q=1' re-parses to query 'q=1'; 'a?b=c' re-parses to path 'a', query 'b=c'. The '%3F' escaping in the both-non-empty case is exactly what makes this true.
input.safeCharacters: Fragment PATH (characters emitted literally, from an exhaustive ASCII 33-126 sweep of D and of A's fragment): A-Z a-z 0-9 ! $ & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; = @ _ ~ — plus '?' ONLY when the fragment query is empty (when the query is non-empty '?' becomes %3F). Percent-encoded in the fragment path: " -> %22, # -> %23, % -> %25, < -> %3C, > -> %3E, ? -> %3F (query non-empty only), [ -> %5B, \ -> %5C, ] -> %5D, ^ -> %5E, ` -> %60, { -> %7B, | -> %7C, } -> %7D, space -> %20. In the fragment QUERY, space -> '+' and '?' -> %3F always. The '?' separator itself and the '#' introducer are the only structural characters emitted raw by the composition step.

uncertainties: The `separator` flag could not be exercised. Nothing in this program sets fragment.separator, and every parse path that (in furl's source) would set it False also leaves the query empty, so the flag never changes the output. I verified across ~40 A values that LINE3 is always 'd?value' — never 'dvalue'. An implementer can omit the flag entirely; if they model it, they must make str() ignore it, otherwise path-only fragments like '#a' would wrongly print 'dvalue' at LINE3.

'#' emission when str(fragment) == '' is NOT directly observable here: LINE3 always forces query='value', so the fragment is never empty at LINE4 (0 of 126 (A,D) combinations produced a LINE4 without '#'). I infer the rule 'emit "#" iff str(fragment) != ""' by analogy with the URL query, where the empty-query cases A='?' and 'http://h/p?#f' demonstrably drop the '?'. This inference is unverified for '#'.

I could not construct a case that distinguishes 'the fragment-path encoder omits %3F when the query is empty' from 'the encoded path string gets .replace("%3F","?") applied when the query is empty'. Both models fit every observation. The replace model is what I recommend, because it also explains 'a?b%3Dc' -> 'a?b%253Dc' (the '?' restored inside a segment that was wholesale-quoted). A distinguishing input would need an encoded path containing the literal 3-char sequence '%3F' not produced by a '?', which seems unreachable since '%' is always encoded to '%25'.
Whether the un-escaping is case-insensitive is untestable: the encoder always emits uppercase hex ('%3f' in the input is normalized to '%3F' on output). Use an exact uppercase replace.

The segment-level encoding quirk seen with '#a?b%3Dc' -> 'a?b%253Dc' (a segment containing a raw '?' appears to be wholesale-quoted, double-encoding an existing '%3D', whereas '#a%3Db' -> 'a=b' decodes normally) belongs to the encoding area, not composition. I observed it but did not fully characterise which segments take the wholesale-quote path; the composition rules above are independent of it.
Non-ASCII / UTF-8 bytes in the fragment were not probed (out of scope for composition); only ASCII 33-126, space, and empty strings were swept.
